prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Memory from EARLIER parts of the document (do not extract facts from it; use it only to resolve names, aliases and who produces an item):
Context: National Airspace System (NAS); Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), airspace users, aircraft, pilots, air traffic controllers, stakeholders, ground/aircraft automation; air traffic management (ATM).
Current ATM predicts trajectories from approved flight plans and scheduled/controlled departures. Sparse exchanged data, unpublished trajectory changes, unsynchronized automation, and tactical “open trajectory” vectors/altitude/speed clearances impair prediction and strategic management. Controllers address separation, weather, and NAS/Traffic Flow Management (TFM) restrictions; actions are not directly communicated to stakeholders/automation. Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departures targeting a Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA) at constraints using user-estimated en-route times without other controller-action knowledge. Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) assumes accurate estimated times of arrival (ETAs).
Management by Trajectory (MBT): FAA and airspace users negotiate four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) for all flights, communicating traffic-management plans. Assigned trajectories must respect user goals and all known NAS constraints from current location to destination; constraint impacts become trajectory constraints. Supported operations include commercial aviation, Unmanned Aircraft Systems, space vehicles, and on-demand air transportation vehicles.
Pilots/controllers use automation to maintain assigned trajectories, including temporal/speed constraints; equipped aircraft bear substantial compliance responsibility. Aircraft operate on closed trajectories wherever possible; improved prediction/coordination enables strategic, closed controller clearances. Resolve uncertainty/disruption by modifying trajectories as early as possible; remaining adjustments are proactive.
All relevant airspace users, aircraft, and FAA automation receive data needed for accurate, consistent 4DT predictions. Publish all trajectory changes; advance trajectory-information exchange between ground automation and aircraft synchronizes predictions. Publish all applicable dynamic (e.g., TFM) and static (e.g., crossing restrictions) NAS constraints for users/automation. Predictability improves demand-capacity alignment and reduces delays.
Trajectory Based Operations (TBO): 4DT-centered NAS vision/evolving endeavors. MBT specifically interprets this vision, resembles four-dimensional (4D) contract concepts, and resolves shortfalls consistently with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO guidance; study refines MBT/TBO.

Document units:
U0042: All constraints affecting a given aircraft are reflected in the 4DT.
U0043: Lack of knowledge about certain types of constraints prevents airspace users from planning business-efficient, acceptable trajectories.
U0044: Those constraints also are unknown to every ground automation system, causing aircraft to be handled with an open- ended clearance when the constraints are encountered.
U0045: Insufficient mechanisms to allow traffic managers and controllers to efficiently and effectively amend flights’ routes cause route amendment backlogs during disruptive NAS events.
U0046: Traffic managers apply constraints to efficiently amend trajectories as NAS events evolve, enabling a more flexible and responsive ATM system that can take full advantage of available airspace and drastically reduce delay.2 There is not a good mechanism that allows controllers and traffic managers to predict the downstream consequences of an action or decision on specific aircrafts’ trajectories.
U0047: Downstream effects of actions on a trajectory are considered in decision making associated with a given trajectory, including tactical control actions.
U0048: By quantifying time-based performance as a metric that complements existing PBN metrics, all IFR aircraft may be managed by a single ATM concept that maximizes efficiency while maintaining an acceptable level of safety risk.
U0049: Current time of arrival control (TOAC) standards establish a minimum performance requirement that some aircraft will be certified for while others will not.
U0050: This type of standard may inadvertently introduce unacceptable safety risk into the NAS and creates a mixed equipage environment in which one ATM concept applies to those who meet the standard while another concept must be applied to those who do not. 1.2 MBT Overview The MBT concept can be summarized by the following key points.  MBT applies to all aircraft operating according to Instrument Flight Rules (IFR).  Aircraft are assigned 4DTs, which are negotiated, closed trajectories, from their current state to their destination.  A NAS Constraint Service publishes common information about NAS constraints to all stakeholders.  Trajectory constraints can be mapped to NAS constraints to facilitate identifying affected aircraft when NAS constraints change.  All aircraft follow their negotiated, assigned trajectories, complying with trajectory constraints.  Trajectory constraints and associated tolerances are defined based on the flight’s individual performance capabilities and the situational need for the constraint. 2 This document does not describe the details of how traffic managers or traffic management automation determines what trajectory constraints to impose on each flight.
